🥳 I built and shipped an app in 2 weeks. Here's what I learned about working with AI:

Pleybook is a contract clause-checker that beats a ChatGPT check. Designed, tested and working. Three things stood out.
1. The AI didn't replace my own knowledge. Frontend, backend, data, infra and UX all came up, and every time I needed to know what quality looked like (e.g even Claude struggles with mobile-friendly design).
2. Testing and QA are what made the speed safe. A Playwright suite and a stubbed LLM provider meant I could move fast and still trust what I shipped.
3. MCPs matter more than clever prompting. Connecting the model directly to the tools I use, like Figma for the design, gave much better results than describing everything in a prompt. The output was a more complete product instead of a demo.

I'm thinking about what to build next. If you're about to build something early-stage, I'm happy to look at it for 20 minutes and tell you what I'd do first. DM me.

❓For those hiring: what would you want to see in a dev who works this way?

Building an interactive 3D simulation like this used to take an external team weeks.
Getting it right still comes down to your underlying setup, not a single magic prompt.

A few years ago, this meant scoping specs, hiring outside specialists, and waiting days to see a rough draft. With the right environment and context in place, this took an afternoon:

🔹 It is the setup, not the prompt
The "one prompt built an app" hype misses the point. If your requirements and architecture are messy, you only generate a fragile demo faster. When that foundation is already structured, you go straight to working output.

🔸 Build vs buy has flipped
For years, buying off the shelf was the only sensible default because custom software took months. You bought a tool and got vendor-locked.

Today? As we say in Arabic, انقلب الوضع رأساً على عقب — things have turned completely on their head. 

You can build and test around your own workflow in hours, instead of signing a multi-year contract on day one.
Own your context first. Build small. Decide whether to buy after.

Use the expensive model once. Then make the cheap ones copy it.

In a workshop for a communications group I asked who used Claude, then who paid for it. About 10% of the room kept their hands up.

That 10% already knows the problem. The best model is the one that burns your credits. On the US$200 plan I pay for, I get about five conversations with the top model. Five.

So here's what I do.

I run the job once, with the best model I have. A communication plan, say. A site analysis. A spec for an app.

Then I keep that result and use it as the reference for the cheaper models. They don't have to invent the plan. They follow it.

It works like hiring a top agency for one job. You pay for the work once, the contract ends, and then you hand that work to a cheaper team and say: do it like this.

The technical names are zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot. Zero-shot means you gave the AI no example, and that's how most people use it. One-shot means one reference. Few-shot means several. The more references it has, the better the result.

You cut cost without cutting quality, because the quality decision was made once, by the model that is good at making it.

Which task would you pay the expensive model to do once, so the cheap ones can copy it? Tell me in the comments.

AI only assists; HR managers must make the final decision.

AI in HR decision-making means algorithms that screen CVs, rank candidates, predict attrition, flag “high potential” talent, or recommend pay and promotion outcomes. Ghanaian banks, telcos, mining firms and fintechs are adopting it fast, because one graduate trainee call can draw thousands of applications. The promise is speed and consistency. The risk is scaling a flaw at industrial volume.

Bias: Amazon famously scrapped a recruiting tool that penalized CVs referencing women’s organizations. The machine did exactly what it was trained to do. Models learn from your history. If a bank’s past hires came mostly from three universities in Accra and Kumasi, the system treats those schools as the definition of talent. Strong candidates from Tamale, Ho or Cape Coast get filtered out before a human sees them. Add gender, age and disability, and the distortion deepens.

Transparency: “The system scored them low” is not an answer a manager can give a rejected candidate. Ghana’s Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843) gives individuals grounds to challenge decisions made solely by automated means. An unexplained score is both a legal exposure and a trust problem.

Where humans must stay in the loop: Anywhere a decision materially changes a person’s livelihood. That means final hiring, termination, promotion, discipline and performance ratings. Termination especially, given your obligations under the Labour Act, 2003 (Act 651). AI informs. People decide, and own it.

What to do
Audit before you deploy. Test outcomes by gender, age, region, institution and disability. If selection rates diverge sharply, fix the model or drop it.

Demand explainability from vendors. No clear reasoning, no contract.
Set decision rights. Automate scheduling and screening logistics. Limit AI to recommending on everything else.

Give candidates an appeal route. A human review channel builds trust and catches errors early.

Train managers to challenge the output. People defer to a confident score.
Efficiency without accountability is just faster risk.
Where is your organization drawing the line between AI-assisted and AI-decided?

I spend a lot of my time signing contracts for work, rentals, etc., and like most people, I'm skeptical about uploading sensitive details to AI. Over the weekend, I explored that idea and built a tool that explains contracts, flags risky clauses, and answers questions while maintaining high privacy.

I wrote 10 invented contracts with 38 planted risks and ran three open models on Groq. All three found between 35 and 37 of them in a single run. The scores were close enough that I don’t treat them as a ranking.

My most useful finding was about prompt injection. I hid a line in one contract telling AI readers the contract was safe to sign. All three models ignored the instruction. Then I asked one of them “is it safe to sign?” and it said yes, quoting the planted line. My quote checker let it through because that sentence really was in the document. The quote checked out and the answer was still wrong.

So I changed a few things:
- The app now spots text aimed at AI readers, warns the user and hides it from the model
- It won’t answer “is it safe to sign?” but always answers factual questions like “is there a late fee?”
- Page numbers and highlights come from my own data, never from the model
- Any flag whose quote isn’t in the document is dropped. In testing this caught 3 invented quotes before a user would have seen them.
There’s still a gap: my detector caught only 3 of 18 new, creatively worded plants, so there’s more work to do there.

On privacy, the public demo runs on a synthetic contract, live uploads are switched off and the app stores nothing. Next I want to add a simple block-and-warn step. It would detect likely personal data like emails, phone numbers, and ID or IBAN-like numbers, and show a warning before analysis with a “continue anyway” option. It’s cheap, honest about what it can’t catch, and doesn’t touch the quote matching.

I’m looking at forward deployed engineering roles, where the job is putting an LLM in front of real users and making it trustworthy. If you’re hiring or know someone who is, I’d love to talk.

"Who owns this decision?" If that question keeps coming up in your company, you need a delegation of authority matrix.
It is a simple table that defines who approves what, and up to which limits: purchasing, payments, hiring, customer discounts, and contracts.
Its value is that daily decisions keep moving without stopping at the owner's desk, while big decisions stay at the right level. It also makes audits easier, because for every approval it is clear who should give it.
Most importantly, it should be reviewed regularly as the company grows, rather than becoming a paper in a drawer.
It is one of the first tools we work on in RIVQAN AI's restructuring engagements.
Our question: do you have a written authority matrix, or do approvals run on habit?

The fastest-growing job title in the UK right now isn't AI Engineer.

It's Founder.

LinkedIn's latest AI Labour Market Update shows UK hiring into Founder roles up 62% year on year (Jul-Sep 2026), with Co-Founder up 14%. That's in a quarter when overall UK hiring was down 12.3%. Among UK Gen Z members, the share adding a founder position rose 59.3%.

Put that next to LinkedIn's 2026 Labor Market Report, which has job transitions globally sitting at a decade low.

Read together, that's a market where fewer people are moving between employers, but more are stepping out of employment altogether to build something of their own.

For anyone running a recruitment or search business, a few things follow:

- Some of your strongest passive candidates now have "Founder" in their headline. If your talent maps quietly filter those people out, your pool is smaller than it needs to be.

- Not every new Founder title is a venture-backed start-up. Some will be independent operators under a new label. The data doesn't separate the two, and that distinction matters a lot to anyone running an interim or contract desk.

- Every new company is a potential client. The question is who those founders are talking to before they make hire number one, not after they have a PSL.

- Founders who come back into employment bring a profile that's hard to place with a title-based brief. Skills, not job titles, will do the matching.

So when clients say candidates aren't moving, is it a supply problem, or has part of the market simply changed what it calls itself?

Before signing off the 2027 budget, try moving a major customer payment back a month. Then move the expected funding round back a quarter. Use those as stress scenarios. See which commitments the business can still afford.

Six assumptions deserve testing before January:

1. Runway
Build a dated cash forecast using funds available for operations, expected collections and committed payments (including payroll, tax, debt repayments and annual bills). Run a case with no new funding.

2. Revenue quality
Separate recurring contracts, one-off projects, paid pilots and unsigned pipeline. Check renewals, delivery margins and collection history.
For Web3 teams, test whether customer activity holds up when token incentives end. For AI teams, check whether paid pilots become renewals at sustainable margins.

3. Customer concentration
Model the largest customer renewing late, spending less or leaving. Calculate the effect on cash and gross profit, alongside the revenue impact.

4. Compute costs
Measure the cost of a successfully completed task, including retries, tools and human review. Test heavy-user workloads and the expiry of cloud credits before committing to pricing or expansion.

5. Vendor dependencies
Review critical cloud, model, data and payment providers: renewal dates, pricing exposure, service limits and switching time. Test the fallback and data export before an outage makes them urgent.

6. Fundraising milestones
Specify what the next round will finance and what evidence you intend to demonstrate, such as renewals, stronger margins or a production rollout. Work backwards from when cash is needed, allowing for delays in diligence and closing.

Put each assumption on one page with:
An owner. Evidence needed. A review date. A trigger for action.

For example: if a major renewal remains unconfirmed at the hiring approval date, revisit the hire before committing the cost.

Then combine the downside assumptions. A late renewal, heavier compute usage and delayed funding can hit together. The plan should make the next decision clearer: which spending proceeds, which waits, and what evidence would change your mind.

Today a company asked for my view on their product. It helps B2B companies grow NRR.
 
My honest answer: most CROs would rather have more pipeline than better NRR.
 
NRR matters. But pipeline is the number that decides whether we hit the year.
 
So this is where I'd point AI agents to build pipeline, whether the deal is €20K or €2M.
 
Watch job posts. A law firm hiring five paralegals for due diligence, or a telco hiring GPU engineers, has just told you what its problem is. An agent can read those every morning.
 
Reopen closed-lost. Many deals were lost on timing. Have an agent check every week what has changed: a new CFO, new funding, a contract up for renewal. It's the cheapest pipeline you'll ever build.
 
Use their words. For a big account, let the agent read the annual report, the earnings call and the tender documents. Use their wording, and you'll get read.
 
Bring something useful. A cost estimate built on their own numbers, or a short review of something they've published. An empty meeting request is easy to ignore.
 
Check what ChatGPT and Claude says about you. Half of software buyers now start their research there. Once a month, ask it the ten questions your buyers ask. If it recommends your competitor, that's your next marketing project.
 
So, CROs: more pipeline or better NRR? Which would you pick?

A founder sent me the pitch of an AI interview tool and asked: "Should we buy this?" So I checked their promises.

🤦‍♀️ "Reads facial expressions and emotions to understand the candidate." 
Ew! A major 2019 psychology review proved that facial expressions do not show what someone actually feels. Even HireVue dropped facial analysis from its screening back in 2021 for the same reason.

🤦‍♀️ "Analyzes the candidate's digital footprint to predict fit."
Are you sure? I always thought that spotting personality traits online and predicting job performance are 2 completely different things, and the pitch deck only shows proof for the first one.

🤦‍♀️ "Every candidate gets the same structured questions and one scoring rubric."
Yep, a structure is good! Until everyone gets forced into the same script. Two strong people for the same role often have different backgrounds, and a bot cannot adjust the questions to fit the person.

I told the founder to go back to the vendor and ask whether their tool just makes the process faster, or predicts performance better? If it's the second, we need the data!

And, how come, the vendor sent back a generic case study about saving recruiter hours, and the founder passed on the contract. The end!

Would you pay for an AI hiring tool to move faster, or only if it predicts better?

Not every business requirement needs to become a permanent hiring decision.
Consider a company preparing for a Salesforce implementation, a cloud migration, an ERP upgrade or a cybersecurity transformation.
The organisation may need highly specialised expertise for a defined period. Once the project reaches completion, that particular skill requirement may reduce significantly.
This is where contract hiring becomes a strategic workforce solution.
Instead of expanding permanent headcount for every specialised requirement, businesses can bring in experienced professionals aligned with specific project needs.
Why are businesses considering project-focused contract hiring?
• Access to Niche Expertise: Bring in professionals with specialised experience that may not be required throughout the year.
• Flexible Workforce Planning: Align team size and skill requirements with different project phases.
• Controlled Resource Commitments: Engage professionals for defined assignments instead of creating permanent positions for temporary requirements.
• Faster Project Mobilisation: Reduce the effort involved in building specialised teams from scratch.
• Better Skill Alignment: Match professionals to the actual technologies, responsibilities and deliverables involved in a project.
Imagine needing a ServiceNow specialist for an implementation, a DevOps engineer for a cloud migration, or a data engineer for a specific analytics initiative.
The requirement is clear. The challenge is finding the right expertise at the right time.

Our focus is on understanding project requirements and connecting businesses with professionals who can contribute to their delivery objectives.
The future of workforce planning is not always about hiring more people. Sometimes, it is about accessing the right expertise exactly when the business needs it.

The UK’s construction and infrastructure pipeline will need around 15,000 more project professionals by 2035, a gap that gets far less attention than the shortage of site trades. Hiring alone won’t close it, because most of the people who will deliver that pipeline are already working in it.

What concerns me more is how thinly the experience to run complex projects is spread. Interface and change management, contract and risk, and execution planning usually sit with a relatively small group of people on any programme, and when that knowledge lives with individuals rather than in how a team works, it leaves when they do.

On Tuesday 1 December, Construction News and @PMI are hosting a webinar on exactly this, Why Hiring Won’t Close Construction’s Delivery Gap. Colin Marrs, editor of Construction News, will chair the discussion with Dr Barbara Marino, Agnieszka Read and my colleague Raphael Ani. 

The panel will look at what the best construction companies in the UK are doing to manage the capability gap. It will also cover how contractors, clients and consultancies turn the expertise of their best people into a standard they can teach and repeat, and where AI can help capture that know-how and where its limits are.

A thought for your soul…

Last week, a recruiter hiring for a 6-month contract role asked me why I had so many job changes and career gaps.

It got me thinking…

As recruiters and TA professionals in the UAE, how many of you have rejected a CV simply because of frequent job changes or gaps?

But have you ever stopped to ask WHY?

Project-based assignments, restructuring, career breaks, changing opportunities… There is often a story behind every move.

And now, with AI becoming part of recruitment, let's not forget one thing:

A CV is a screening tool. It's a first impression, NOT the whole story.

AI can match keywords. A CV can show experience. But neither can replace a meaningful conversation to understand the person behind the profile.

After all, aren't we in the business of hiring people, not just matching CVs?

Before rejecting the CV, have the conversation. You might be overlooking the right talent.

What's your take?
